One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, is moon-colored, has four arms,
and possesses a serene countenance, for the pacification of all obstacles.
Salutation to the Great Lord of the Host. The year of Īśvara. The month of Āṣāḍha. Sunday.
(Cosapēṭṭai Subramanya Gurukkal).
(Line 2) Written and engraved by Śirakuraṇṭam Subramanyaṉ.
The commencement of the worship for the sake of others:

having approached in the presence of the protector of the field (*kṣetrapāla*), and having performed the worship of the door, one should offer the bath and other consecrations, worship, food offerings (*naivedya*), incense, lamps, and water for honor (*arghya*), and then make a supplication.
O Lord, guardians of the field for the protection of all the world upon earth,
grant me a staff with its seal for the purpose of performing the ritual worship of Śiva.

Thus, having taken up the weapon of the *aṅkuśa* mudrā and approached the door of the bedchamber, one should have the Rudra-attendants perform song and instrumental music at the side of the door for the purpose of opening the eyes of Śiva and Śakti. Having performed the worship of the door and opened the panels, and having warded off the three obstacles, one should enter within. Having sprinkled the curtain that conceals the couch with water for the *arghya* offering while reciting the *astra-mantra*, and having worshipped it with the *varma-mantra*, one should place it above the couch.

Having projected the form with the *astra* mantra, having sprinkled [it] and discarded the remains of the previous offering (*nirmālya*), and having given water with the *astra* mantra for the purification of the feet and hands; having sprinkled [the deity] with the *arghya* water using the root mantra (*mūla*) for the purpose of bathing; having adorned [it] with perfumes, garlands, and so forth using the *astra* mantra; having worshipped [it] with the root, *brahma*, and limb-mantras (*aṅga-mantra*); and having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, lamp, and *arghya*; one should place the Lord upon a palanquin without [excessive] force, and accompanied by all musical instruments and attendants, approach the vicinity of the temple (*liṅga-sannidhi*).

Having joined that form to the *liṅga* with a flower and the *udbhava-mudrā*, one should install the form in its proper place. For the purpose of worship, having stood upon the tortoise-seat (*kūrma-āsana*) in the bathing pavilion (*snāpana-maṇṭapa*), one should perform the purification of the site (*sthāna-śuddhi*). Having sprinkled it with *arghya* water and, with the *astra-mantra*, drawn a square measuring only a *tritala*, one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the Goddess of the Earth (*bhūmi-devī*) with the seat and other offerings. As for the visualization (*dhyāna*):
she has two arms and two eyes, and is adorned with a basket-shaped crown (*karaṇḍa-mukuṭa*).

Having meditated thus: "The Goddess, adorned with all ornaments, [bestowing] the boons of the *vara* and *abhaya* mudrās," she should be worshipped with the Heart-mantra and the Weapon-mantra. Having offered the food offering (*naivedya*) and the water for honor (*arghya*), this is the purification of the site (*sthalaśuddhi*). The conch, the vessel for the command (*ājñā*), the vessel for water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), the vessels for water for the feet (*pādya*), and the flower-vessels should be washed with the Weapon-mantra and established with the Heart-mantra. They should be inspected and prepared with clay. One should fill the *vardhanī* vessel and the conch-vessel with water using the Root-mantra, worship the *vardhanī* with the Śiva-weapon mantra, and consecrate it by worshipping it with the Brahma-mantras and the limb-mantras (*aṅga*).

Having displayed the *liṅgapadmamudrā* and performed the fivefold purification (*pañcaśuddhi*) of the conch water, one should worship it with the root mantra. Having consecrated it eleven times with the ten-syllable seed-mantra, one should display the *dhenu*, *astra*, and *mahāmudrās*. Having offered incense and lamps, one should sprinkle the ritual substances (*dravyas*) with that water and prepare the vessels for the special *arghya*, *pādya*, and *ācamanīya*. Having placed the excellent substances within them, one should worship the *arghya* water with the *astra* and *brahmāṅga* mantras.

Having worshipped the vessel for water for the feet with the *hṛdaya* mantra and consecrated it seven times with the *praṇava*, [one should likewise treat] the vessel for water for sipping and the vessel for the *arghya* offering.

Having worshipped with the ten [mantras], having consecrated it with the *savya* [mantra], having displayed the *dhenumudrā*, and having offered incense and lamps—this is the purification of the substances (*dravyaśuddhi*). For the purpose of invoking the Hand of Śiva (*śivahasta*), one should place sandalwood paste, flowers, and unbroken rice grains upon the palm of the right hand with the root mantra. Having performed the rites beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and ending with the transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) with the left hand, one should worship the form of the seat consisting of Dharma and the other [qualities]. Having applied the root mantra and the *brahmāṅga* mantras, and having meditated on [the deity] as having the form of light, one should deposit [the Hand of Śiva] upon the head with the Śiva-mantra.
Having observed with divine vision by means of the *prāsāda* [mantra] for a distance of two cubits, one should contemplate the hand of Śiva.
Then, as for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*):
having prepared a square measuring one cubit in the western part with rice grains, one should proceed.
In the Ajita [tantra],

on the tip, middle, and root of the Veda [four] lines drawn to the left, there are squares according to the rule of the number of principles (*tattva*) in groups of five. There, having set aside the first rule, one should add the second row.
First, the number of seeds and subsequent joys (*uttarananda*) is thus delineated. In the central square: *oṃ hāṃ śivatattvakoṣṭhāya namaḥ*.
In the southeast: *īśvaratattvakoṣṭhāya namaḥ*.
Salutation to the square of the principle of Māyā in the southwest.
Salutation to the square of the principle of Sadāśiva in the east.
To the Vidya-tattva square in the south, obeisance.
To the Puruṣa-tattva square in the north, obeisance. To the Kāla-tattva square in the west, obeisance. (p. 9a blank)
In the northwest, homage to the square of the principle of necessity (*niyatitatva*). In the northeast, homage to the square of the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛtitatva*).

In this manner, the receptacles are to be worshipped. They are to be encircled with the *navasūtra* (nine-fold thread), worshipped, rinsed in the heart [mantra], sprinkled with the *astra* [mantra], and offered incense, lamps, and *arghya* with the *varma* [mantra]. Having placed the vessels in the center of the receptacle:
in the middle, "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the well-established vessel (*supratiṣṭhapātra*). In the east, "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the well-pacified vessel (*suśāntapātra*)."
In the south: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the vessel of radiant splendor.
(L.3) In the north: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the vessel of jewel-water.
In the west: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the vessel whose nature is nectar.

In the northeast: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the vessel of the Unmanifest.* From the southeast to the northwest: *Obeisance to the vessel consisting of nectar.* Having thus worshipped and adorned [the vessels] with perfumes and other offerings, [one should worship] at the back, middle, and front parts of the central vessel.

One should worship the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra. To its east and ending in the north, one should worship Gaṇapati, the Six-faced One (Kārttikeya), Nandin, and Mahākāla. In the intermediate directions, one should worship the four Vedas. Having honored them and offered incense, lamps, and *arghya*, one should fill the central vessel with milk using the mantra "Āpyāyasva. In the east, [one should place] curd using the mantra "Dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam."
On the right—
fill the vessel of Śukra with clarified butter.
In the north—with the *sāvitrī* mantra—cow’s urine;
in the west—with *gandhadvārā*—cow dung;
in the northeast—with *devasya tvā*—kuśa-water.

From the southeast (āgneya) to the northwest (vāyavya), one should place the substances of oil, feces, and myrobalan (āmalaka) with the Astra-mantra. Having arranged the tuft of hair (kūrca), sprouts, gems, and coconuts, one should sprinkle them with the "water of the auspicious day" (puṇyāha-jala).

Having consecrated [the substances] five times—starting from milk and ending with *kuśa* water—in five vessels using the mantra "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām," one should invoke [the deity]. Having displayed the mudrās as prescribed, and having offered food (*naivedya*), incense (*dhūpa*), lamp (*dīpa*), and the water-offering (*arghya*), one should worship the other vessels with the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) mantra. Having displayed the mudrās, one should consecrate [the substances] starting from milk and ending with *kuśa* water, and starting from oil and ending with turmeric (*rajanī*), using the root-mantra, the Brahma-mantras, the *vyāhṛtis*, the ten seed-syllables, and the sequential mantras.

The substances contained in the five vessels starting from the east should be combined, in due order, into the central vessel. Having recited the *mūla-mantra* one hundred and eight times, and having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and the sprinkling (*avakuṇṭhana*), one should perform the purification (*nirmadhyā*) three times with the mantra *mā nastoke*. Holding the tip of the nose with both the left and right hands without exhaling, one should lift [the substance] and establish it with the *mūla-mantra*. Thus one should worship the *pañcagavya*.

Then, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with *śāli* rice on the western side for the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), one should arrange nine squares in the center and discard four squares starting from the southeast (*āgneya*).
In the center square: *oṃ hāṃ pṛthvī-tattva-koṣṭhāya namaḥ*.
In the east: *oṃ hāṃ ap-tattva-koṣṭhāya namaḥ*. In the south: *oṃ hāṃ vahni-tattva-koṣṭhāya namaḥ*.
In the west: *oṃ hāṃ vāyutattvakoṣṭhāya namaḥ*.
In the north: *oṃ hāṃ vyomatattvakoṣṭhāya namaḥ*.
Having thus worshipped them, one should wrap the vessels with thread and wash them with the *astra-mantra*.
Having kindled [the lamps] with the heart-mantra and having placed the vessels in the compartments:
*Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to the vessel of the element of fragrance for the western direction;
to the east, obeisance to the vessel of the element of taste.

To the south—salutation to the vessel of the principle of form (rūpa-tattva-pātra). To the west—salutation to the vessel of the principle of touch (sparśa-tattva-pātra). To the north—salutation to the vessel of the principle of sound (śabda-tattva-pātra).
Thus, having performed the worship.

In the center, milk; in the east, fruit; in the south, honey or clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*); in the west, sugar or jaggery (*guḍa*); in the north, sugarcane juice, coconut water, or *balila*. Having worshipped with the Brahma-mantras as before, having consecrated it with the limbs of Brahmā, and having invoked [the deity], one should display the five mudrās. Having offered incense, lamps, and the *arghya* offering, one should combine the substances situated in the vessels in the four directions—starting from the east—into the central vessel. One should then consecrate it with the root mantra (*mūla*).

Having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), one should consecrate [the materials] with the Vedic *brahmāṅga* mantras; this is the *pañcāmṛta* bath. To the west of that, upon three *droṇas* of rice, sesame, and grain, at a height of five *tālas*, having drawn a square and a lotus, one should worship a lotus seat (*padmāsana*) upon it. Having wound nine jars with a *vardhanī* thread, having washed them with the *hṛdaya* mantra, having fumigated them with the *astra* mantra, and having filled them with water, [one should fill them] with fragrant substances, gems, *kūrca* grass, sprouts, coconut fruit, flowers, and so forth.

Having adorned [the deity] with perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and cloth, and having established it upon a lotus with the *astra-mantra*, one should worship it. Having worshipped the form of the seat of Śiva in the center, one should invoke [the deity]. Having performed the rites of installation (*sthāpana*) and so forth, one should display the five mudrās. One should invoke Manonmanī into the *vardhanī* vessel with the mantra; having performed the rites of installation and so forth, one should display the *padmayoni-mahāmudrā*. In the eight directions beginning with the east, one should worship [the deities] starting from Ananteśa and ending with Śikhaṇḍin. Having offered food offerings (*naivedya*) and so forth, as well as incense, lamps, and water for honor (*arghya*), one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* and the sequence of the *kalās*.

The Bathing. Now, for the worship of the Sun: one should worship Śiva-Sūrya in the northeast, between Indra and Agni. Having offered the *arghya* with the *praṇava* as the seat while facing north in front of the Sun, one should install [the deity]. On the right and left sides of the door: "Salutation to Daṇḍin; salutation to Piṅgala; salutation to Gaṇapati; salutation to the Gurus. Having entered within, on the seat: "Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Prabhūtāsana. In the inner enclosure (*garbhāvaraṇa*), from the southwest to the northeast: "Salutation to Vimala; salutation to Sāra; salutation to Purādhyāya."

Homage to Supreme Bliss (*paramasukha*). Homage to Padma. Having thus displayed the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*), [one offers homage] from the front of its face toward the eight directions: Homage to Dīptā; homage to Sūkṣmā; homage to Jayā; homage to Bhadrā; homage to Vibhūti; homage to Vimalā; homage to Amoghā; homage to Vidyutā; homage to Sarvatomukhī. Having displayed the radiating mudrā (*visphuramudrā*), [one says]: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Sun Throne (*arkāsana*).

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Sun-form (*arkamūrti*). Oṃ ghaṃ (khaṃ khaṣolkāya), obeisance to Ghaṣolka, the Sun-form. Oṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the eyes. Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Sahasraśiva-sūrya. Having invoked [the deity] with this mantra, one should display the five mudrās beginning with the *sthāpanā*. Having offered incense, lamps, and the *arghya* offering, one should meditate as follows: "I bow to Āditya, the creator of all, endowed with twelve digits, holding two lotuses in his hands, the sole witness of all the worlds. Having thus meditated—

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *gāyatrī*, one should worship the limbs (*aṅga*). Having consecrated the image with water containing *janman* [seeds], and having again consecrated it with water containing all substances such as oil and so forth, and having adorned it, one should worship it with the root mantra. Having displayed the *padmavisphura-yonimudrā*, one should worship Uṣā and Pratyuṣā on its two sides. One should worship the planets, beginning with Soma, in the eight directions of its circular perimeter.

In the third enclosure, one should worship the ten world-protectors (lokapālas), having offered food offerings (naivedya), incense, lamps, and water for honor (arghya). On the left, one should worship Oṃ Hāṃ Tejaścaṇḍeśvara. Then, having projected the form [of the deity] into the heart by means of the root mantra, one should perform a salutation. Thus ends the worship of the Sun.

Now, the worship of Gaṇeśa: having sat with a serene face in the pavilion in front of Gaṇeśa, and having performed the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and other rites, as well as the ritual of the limbs (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should perform the ceremonial sipping of water (*ācamana*) and apply the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*).
[With] "Oṃ *gaṃ*, obeisance to the Lord of All," one places it on the head. [With] "Oṃ *gaṃ*, obeisance to the Destroyer of Obstacles," one places it on the eyes.
Oṃ gaṃ, obeisance to the elephant-faced one—at the waist. Oṃ gaiṃ, obeisance to the one whose vehicle is a rat—at the thighs. Oṃ gauṃ, obeisance to Vighneśvara—at the knees. (l. 5)
"Oṃ gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇeśvara"—thus [one places the mantra] on the two feet.

Again, having performed the *arghya* placement on the head, face, chest, private parts, knees, and feet with the five mantras beginning with "gaṇān tvā," and having performed the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) rite—this is the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*). Then, having prepared the vessels for *arghya*, *pādya*, and *ācamanīya* as before, and having performed the rites from the merit-rite (*puṇyāha*) up to the bathing (*snāna*).
Having sprinkled the door with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*),
one should worship Gaṇanapati, Sarasvatī, and Mahālakṣmī above;
on both sides, one should worship Bhuvaṅga, Pataṅga, Kūśmāṇḍa, and Kumbhodara, ending each name with "namaḥ."

Having worshipped with the root-mantra (*mūla*) at the jeweled cavity (*maṇivila*), and having performed the worship ending with the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), one should apply the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and so forth at their respective locations using the seed-syllables (*bīja*). Having invoked with the root-mantra and having assigned the *Gāyatrī* mantra and the [principal] mantra, one should worship the door-keepers and, in front, worship the great demon-rat (*mahāsuramūṣika*). Having performed the ritual services (*upacāra*), one enters within. From the southwest (*naiṛtya*) to the northeast (*īśāna*), one worships Vāsudeva, Sarasvatī, Mahālakṣmī, Samṛddhi, and Vijayā. Having displayed the noose (*pāśa*), goad (*aṅkuśa*), triple-sectioned (*trikhaṇḍa*), and womb (*yonimudrā*) gestures, one performs the meditation (*dhyāna*).

Having meditated upon the elephant-faced one, who has three eyes, the luster of saffron, and four arms—holding a noose and a tusk in his right hands, and a goad and a sweetmeat (*laḍḍuka*) in his left hands—and having consecrated him with water containing the substances prescribed for bathing, such as oil for massage and so forth, and having adorned him with garments and other ornaments, one should worship him as before. On both sides, one should honor Siddhilakṣmī and her beloveds. In the second enclosure, one should worship the forms of Gaṇeśa.
Born of Yoga:
Vighneśa, Mahākarṇa, Gajavaktra, and Mahodara.
The one with a single tusk, of massive body, the lord of the host of Vināyakas.
Thus she is to be worshipped. In the third enclosure,
according to the *Cintya-tantra*,
the Child (*bāla*), the Devotee (*bhakta*), the Hero (*vīra*), and the Power (*śakti*) bestow the accomplishment of all aims.
Piṅgala, Ciṣṭharakta, Ākṣipra, and Heramba;
Lakṣmījaya, Nṛtta, Ūrdhva, and Mahāgaṇa— these sixteen, beginning with Haridra, one should worship as the third group.
In the fourth enclosure, in the southeast at the foot of the *santāna* tree: salutation to Brahmā accompanied by Sarasvatī.
In the southwest at the foot of the *mandāra* tree: salutation to Viṣṇu accompanied by Lakṣmī.
In the northwest, at the foot of a *kalpataru* tree: salutation to Maheśvara accompanied by Bhavānī.
In the northeast, at the foot of a sandalwood tree: salutation to Kāmadeva accompanied by Rati.

Having worshipped Indra and the other world-protectors (*lokapālas*) in the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*), and having offered various kinds of food offerings (*naivedya*) such as coconuts and so forth, up to sweetmeats (*modaka*) and sugar-balls (*laḍḍuka*), along with incense, lamps, and water for honor (*arghya*), [one should offer] the divine oblation (*devabali*) to the guardians of the gates and others in the eight directions beginning with the north.

Having placed [the offering] on the sacrificial pedestal (*balipīṭha*) with the words, "Homage to the one who causes all obstacles," and having worshipped [him], one should offer the oblation (*bali*) with "Oṃ, svāhā to the hosts of all obstacle-makers. Having cast the *arghya* water for the obstruction at the front and performed all the ritual services (*upacāra*), this concludes the worship of Vighneśvara. Then, having approached the door of the deity:

On the right side, having worshipped Gaṇapati with offerings such as coconut and other articles, (l. 3) ... having sprinkled the door with water for the *arghya* using the *astra-mantra*, and having placed flowers in the south, north, and middle; one should worship Gaṇapati, Sarasvatī, and Mahālakṣmī in the upper, southern, northern, and middle positions respectively. On the right side: "Salutation to Nandin, salutation to Gaṅgā. On the left side: "Salutation to Mahākāla, salutation to Yamunā."

In the lower and upper [sections] of the wall: *namaḥ* to Bhuvaṅga; *namaḥ* to the two Pataṅgas. In the hollow (*suṣira*), one should worship the nine powers (*navaśakti*). In front: *namaḥ* to the Weapon (*astra*). On the right side of the wall: *namaḥ* to the weapon-bearing door-guardian (*dvārapāla*) Ḍiṇḍin.
His form is like the rays of the rising sun, his face is terrible, and he has three eyes.
With his matted locks and deer-face positioned above, he has his feet placed upward with his face turned upwards.

"I worship the form of Dindi, whose pair of hands are blossomed, who holds a staff in his hand of wonder, and who is adorned with a garland of victory-jewels. Having thus meditated, [one should place] on the northern side: "Obeisance to Muṇḍin, the guardian of the weapon-gate."
His body is like that of a python, his face is terrifying, and his matted hair stands erect;
his arms are outstretched like staffs, with hands displaying the *vāstu-mudrā*;
he has a noose fastened around his waist, wears bracelets, and is adorned with serpents.

"I worship the form of Muṇḍī, who is served by sages, gods, and men. Having meditated thus, and having offered the *arghya* (to the deity), [having offered the *arghya*] before Vṛṣabheśvara, obeisance.
Meditation.
His body is like silver, his feet are the Vedas, and his face is turned upward;
he has reddish-hued, rising horns, the color of fire, and three eyes.
He is adorned with a garland of victory-gems and decorated with a string of tinkling bells.

Having meditated thus: "The primordial deity, the bull, whose form is the Dharma of green body," one should worship with the root mantra. Then, having invoked [the deity] with the mantra "O excellent bull" (*yastu śṛṅgaḥ suvṛṣabha*), and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the Gāyatrī, one should offer the food offering (*naivedya*) to all. Having warded off the three kinds of obstacles—those dwelling in the divine realm, the intermediate space, and on the earth—at the vicinity of the door.
One should look into the sky with divine vision.

Having cast flowers into the intermediate space with the *nārāca-mudrā* while reciting "āstrāya huṃ phaṭ," and having touched the ground three times with the big toe of the right foot while reciting the *astra-mantra*,
one should strike the bell three times with the *astra-mantra* for the purpose of dispelling the three obstacles.
Having entered within with the Sadyojāta [mantra] from the southern foot toward the northern side,
[one should place it] on the crown.
The deities stationed above the door have natural faces during worship;
at the time following the offering of the bali-oblation, they invariably have distorted faces.
Having spread out the torn cloth with the heart-mantra: "Homage to Sthāṇu.
Meditation.

"Mounted upon a blue horse, adorned with garments, garlands, and ornaments, she who has shrouded the three worlds in sleep—[I worship her] who bears the *khaḍvāṅga*. Having thus meditated (line 5), one should perform worship. Having entered the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), one should sprinkle the threshold of the inner sanctum with the Weapon-mantra (*astramantra*). One should worship the enclosure of the inner sanctum starting from the southwest direction (*nairṛtī*) up to the end of the north.

In the southwest, one should worship that Brahmā with the mantra "iti mantreṇa" and the formula "vāstvādhipataye namaḥ. In the west, one should worship Gaṇapati as Niṣustim with the mantra "gaṇapateti. In the northwest, one should worship Sarasvatī with the mantra "praṇate sarasvatī."

In the north, one should worship Lakṣmī with the mantra beginning "hiraṇyavarṇām. At the mouth of the cow, one should worship the goddess Vāc with the mantra [beginning] "vācam," and then worship the nine powers, Vāmā and the others. (l.2) In the northeast, with the mantra "saṃbrahmam," one should worship Sadāśiva, Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, and again Ambikā;
furthermore, one should worship Guha, Viṣṇu, Vidhātṛ, and the Guru—these seven. (l.3)

Thus, having worshipped the seven *gurus*, having gathered [the materials] with the *astra-mantra*, and having filled [the vessel] with water by means of the *mūla-mantra*, one should invoke the *naisthika* [deity] into its midst with the mantra "imaṃ me gaṅge". Having offered incense, lamps, and the *arghya* offering, one should recite the *brahmāṅga-mantra* once. Having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with the *astra-mantra* and consecrated [the water] with the *mūla-mantra*, one should sprinkle it with water. One should worship Rudra upon the head of the *liṅga* with the *yo nidrayati* mantra.

Having gathered the *nirmālya* with the thumb and forefinger, one should place it in the northeastern direction (*īśāna*) with the mantra "namo vaḥ kirikebhyaḥ. Then, having sprinkled the *liṅga* with the water of the *arghya* offering using the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) "pramuñca dhanvaṃs tvam," and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should wash the *liṅga* with the mantra:

"Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ paṃ śuṃ (huṃ) phaṭ pāśupatāstrāya namaḥ. Finally, with the root-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should [clean] the *liṅga* and the pedestal (*piṭha*) with a *kūrca* brush. Thus ends the purification of the *liṅga*.

One should contemplate [the deity] upon the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) situated at the *mūlādhāra*. Having applied a tilaka on the forehead with green sandalwood paste, one should place a flower on the crest-lock (*śikhā*) with the root-mantra. For the sake of removing impurity from the mantras, one should exhale through the *kumbhaka* breath-control, drawing [the breath] from the base to the top of the head via the *suṣumnā* up to the end of the *nāda*. One should recite the *Śiva-mantra* ten times. One should consecrate the limbs of Brahmā once; this is the purification of the mantras.
Due to the movement of the teeth and lips during the ritual procedure (*kalpa*), the mantras have become impure.
The utterance of the end of the *nāda* is taught as the means for avoiding those defects.
(l. 5) Now, the five seats: on the foundation stone (*ādhāraśilā*), "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Foundation Power (*ādhāraśakti*)".
Seated upon the tortoise-stone below, her body white as the ocean of milk.

Having meditated thus: "The primordial Śakti, whose form is that of the seed and the sprout, who bestows boons and fearlessness, who holds a noose and a goad, who is the power (kriyā) and the very nature of the support"—
this is the meditation (dhyāna).

On the *brahmaśilā*, one should worship Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Kārkoṭaka, and Śaṅkhapāla in the four directions starting from the east; then, from the southeast to the northeast, one should worship Gulika, Padma, and Mahāpadma.

"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Anantāsana"—thus [one worships] Anantāsana. ... [From] the eastern panel to the golden corner, having visualized the lion-throne (siṃhāsana), one should worship from the southeast to the northeast: "Salutation to Dharma," "Salutation to Jñāna," "Salutation to Vairāgya," "Salutation to Aiśvarya. Having worshipped Jñāna and Vairāgya, and having worshipped Aiśvarya, [one worships] from its east to the north: "Salutation to Adharma," "Salutation to Ajñāna," "Salutation to Avairāgya," "Salutation to Anaiśvarya."

One should abandon unrighteousness (*adharma*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), lack of dispassion (*avairāgya*), and lack of sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*). Having worshipped the *rājasa*, *sāttvika*, and *tāmasa* [forms] in the right, left, and middle [positions] starting from the upper ear... then in the four directions beginning with the southeast (*āgneyī*), one should worship the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages. In the center: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lion Throne (*siṃhāsana*). Now, for the yoga-seat (*yogāsana*), from the upper throat upwards to the end of the upper band, in the middle between the northeast (*īśāna*) and the north (*udīcī*), [one says]: "Salutation to the Unmanifest (*avyakta*). In the middle between the south (*dakṣiṇa*) and the southeast (*āgneya*), [one says]: "Salutation to the Restrained (*niyata*). (Page 17a, line 1)

One should worship with: "Obeisance to Kāla in the middle of Nairṛti and Varuṇa; obeisance to Keśava in the middle of Vāyu and Soma. Then: "Obeisance to the lower covering in the southwest (Nairṛta); obeisance to the upper covering in the northeast (Īśāna); Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the Yoga-seat in the northeast"—thus [one worships] the Yoga-seat. Having visualized the blossomed lotus-seat upon the upper plank... [one contemplates] in the region of the *mūlādhāra*, from the east to the northeast, [the seat] consisting of the sprout of the seed-syllable of the *kanda*, like coconut water, extending to the petals, filaments, and pericarp.

They are to be worshipped in the eight directions. In the center: *oṃ hāṃ padmāsanāya namaḥ*. On the eight petals, one should worship the eight Śaktis: *namaḥ vāmāyai*; *oṃ hāṃ jyeṣṭhāyai namaḥ*; *namaḥ raudryai*; *namaḥ kālyai*; *namaḥ kalavikaraṇyai*; *namaḥ balavikaraṇyai*; *namaḥ balapramathanyai*; *namaḥ sarvabhūtadamanyai*. In the pericarp: *namaḥ manonmanyai*. Then, one should display the gesture of salutation (*namaskāramudrā*).

Within the filaments at the tips of the petals, one should contemplate three circles extending from the tip of each filament to its middle base. On the right side of the upper circle: *ātmatattvāya namaḥ*; *brahmaṇe ātmatattvādhipataye namaḥ*.

On the left: *vidyātattvāya namaḥ*; *viṣṇave vidyātattvādhipataye namaḥ*. In the center: *śivatattvāya namaḥ*; *rudrāya śivatattvādhipataye namaḥ*. Having visualized the pericarp in the midst of the ghee and water, one should contemplate it within that mandala.

In the first circle: *Namaḥ* to the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*). *Namaḥ* to Brahmā, the presiding lord of the solar disc. *Namaḥ* to the lunar disc (*somamaṇḍala*). *Namaḥ* to Viṣṇu, the presiding lord of the lunar disc. *Namaḥ* to the fiery disc (*agnimaṇḍala*). *Namaḥ* to Rudra, the presiding lord of the fiery disc. Having visualized the Sadāśiva-maṇḍala for the sake of a seat above the base of the Rudra-portion on top of the liṅga situated within that [fiery] disc: having meditated... (l. 6) ...on the right, [one says]: *Oṃ hāṃ, namaḥ* to the Sadāśiva-maṇḍala. *Namaḥ* to Śakti, the presiding lord of the Sadāśiva-maṇḍala.
Meditation upon the great and vast [deity] in divine form,
together with the seed-syllable in the heart, which illuminates all mantras.
"Even though he is great, he is pure knowledge within the *manas*; I bow to that beauty which flows forth even once. Having meditated thus, (p.18a, l.1).
...thus, having worshipped Śakti;
and having performed the third portion of the worship for the Kāraṇa, [one should perform] the half-portion for the Rudra.
One should worship Madhyabhāgeśvara and Sadāśiva in the front portion.
One should worship Sāman, Ravi, Śakti, Śiva, Śakti,
and Suvāsana above the portion of Rudra; one should divide that portion by the number five,
and having worshipped the maṇḍala, [one should worship] the cause consisting of the five...thakāras.
Below this, in the portion of Viṣṇu, one should likewise worship Padmayogāsana;
then, in the portion of Brahmā, one should well-worship Siṃhāsana.
Maheśvara [should be worshipped] in the [remaining] portion, and Sadāśiva in the front region.
One should worship with the "staff-breaking" gesture (*daṇḍabhaṅgī*) and so forth, and perform the "viṇā-limb" and "shaven-head" rites.

Thus, one should worship in this sequence: *Oṃ hāṃ śaktimaṇḍalāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ śaktimaṇḍalādhipataye īśvarāya namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped, [one proceeds] in the center: *Oṃ hāṃ vimalāsanāya namaḥ*; these are the five seats (*pañcāsana*). Above that, in the portion of Sadāśiva: *Śivāsanāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ śivamūrttaye namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ vidyādehāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ vidyādehanetrebhyo namaḥ*.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva," one should worship the five Brahmans and their limbs, beginning with Īśāna, in the sequence of the *muṇḍabhaṅgī* [head-arrangement]. Having worshipped the *yoga* for the purpose of invocation in the *kāraṇa*, one should place a single flower in the left hand while reciting the root mantra. (l. 2)

Having performed the fivefold purification (*pañcaśuddhi*), one should place the seed-syllables of the five Brahmans—beginning with *Sammiśraṇa* and ending with *Sadyojāta*—from the thumb to the little finger. Then, having placed the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) from the little finger to the thumb using their respective long seed-syllables, one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with the weapon-mantra (*astra*). Having displayed the *añjali* mudrā and meditated upon Sadāśiva, [one should assign] the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*) to the seat of invocation and yoga;
for worship, the great lotus (*mahāpadma*); and for the meal, that which is called "the stainless" (*vimala*).
In hymns, dance, and song, one is liberated accordingly.
[He who has] five faces resembling the moon, ten hands, and holds a spear,
a seal-ring, a sword, a thunderbolt, and the gesture of fearlessness— [he is the Lord].
Having meditated [on him] as having a noose, the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), a goad, and a jewel in his left hands,
and as being seated upon a white lotus in the form of Sadāśiva— thus, according to the *Kāmika*.
The sequence for the rite of invocation of the Svayambhūdevis,
as well as the consecration and the ritual application of the limbs of the Liṅga, is thus remembered.

The invocation is performed with the *anyaliṅga* [mantra]. Having meditated upon the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Maheśvara, and Paramaśiva at the heart, throat, tip of the cloth, between the eyebrows, the crown of the head, and the station of the *dvādaśānta* by means of the *prāsāda* [mantra], one should unify them through *recaka* [exhalation]. Having joined *sadaśiva* upon the flower placed during *kumbhaka* [retention], and having meditated upon that [deity] as possessing the brilliance of ten million moons, one should bring the hands together in *añjali* level with the heart, meditate upon it in the form of a *bindu*, and place it upon the tip of the cloth.

Having gazed with divine vision while exhaling (*recaka*), one should invoke the Flower (*prasūna*)—arisen from the Heart-toe Gesture (*hṛdayastobhamudrā*)—above the head of the *liṅga* with the root mantra ending in *namaḥ*. Having established it upon the right shoulder, one should perform the placement of the Brahma-limbs (*brahmāṅga*) according to the sequence of the Staff-formation (*daṇḍabhaṅgī*). Having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and the nectarization (*amṛtīkṛta*), one should offer the water of honor (*arghya*) with the root mantra to the five faces and six limbs. Having performed the placement of the five Brahmans (*pañcabrahman*) from the head down to the region of Rudra according to the sequence of the Staff-formation, one should place the Form of Śiva (*śivamūrti*) and the Body of Knowledge (*vidyādeha*) in the place of Maheśvara. [One should then perform] the Eye-gesture (*netramudrā*) with the limb of Śiva.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the three eyes; having performed the placement of the five [mantras] of Īśāna, beginning from the head and ending at the private parts (*rudrabhaga*); having again prepared the seat of Śiva (*śivāsana*); having performed the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in their respective locations; having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and the nectar-ification (*amṛtīkaraṇa*); having performed the placement according to the sequence of the forms of the *mātṛkā* and the *kalās*; immediately thereafter, having placed a flower in the hand; and having formed the mudrās starting with the five purifications (*pañcaśuddhi*) as before—[one recites] "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām" and "Sadyojātam."

It has been stated that [the rite] begins with the east; one should perform the invocation in sequence, followed by the installation (*sthāpana*) and so forth, and having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the mantras beginning with the Heart-mantra. "Homage to you, the *kirikas*" is the installation (*sthāpana*). "In this great ocean... is the presence (*sannidhāna*). "That which goes... is the confinement (*sannirodhana*). "He has spoken... is the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*). "We worship Tryambaka" is the supreme consecration (*paramīkaraṇa*).

Having performed the binding of the directions with the mantra *pramuñca dhanvana*, and having offered the *arghya* water, one should present three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) while reciting the *Śivagāyatrī* mantra. Then, at the five faces [of the deity], beginning with Īśāna, one should display the five mudrās using the five mantras, starting from the center.

With the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). Having displayed the great *añjali* with five faces: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śiva"—thus [offering] the water for the feet (*pādya*). "Oṃ hāṃ, to Śiva sva-dhe-ti"—thus the water for sipping (*ācamana*). "Oṃ hāṃ, to Śiva svāhā"—thus the water of honor (*arghya*). Having offered the water for the feet, the water for sipping, the water of honor, and so forth, along with incense and lamps, one should recite the mantra of the verse from the *Rudrasūkta* and other such hymns once; this is the invocation (*āvāhana*). Then, having worshipped the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*) for the sake of [the deity's] arrival, and having placed a flower upon the top of the *liṅga* with the root-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should pray to the God: "O God of gods, Lord of the world, whose nature consists of five faces..."
For the sake of the consecration for protecting the day, face upwards.

Having thus prayed, one should take the vessel for consecration with the root mantra (*mūla*). Having worshipped the mandalas of the Moon, Sun, and Fire upon the back, middle, and the eight directions of the vessel, and having consecrated it with the root mantra, one should perform the consecration after observing a time devoid of the Moon and Sun.
In the *Bhīmasaṃhitā* it is said:
"Worship at a time when the Moon, Sun, and Fire are absent bestows all accomplishments."
If one performs a sacrifice at a time devoid of that [proper] moment, it shall be fruitless.
The vital breath is thus the sun, and the vital breath is also the moon; having brought about the cessation of these two, it is known as being devoid of both moon and sun.

Thus, having gradually restrained the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) from above and below, one should take water filled to the count of the *kālottara* [breaths] from the pitcher, mixed with fragrance, by means of inhalation (*pūraka*). Then, by means of exhalation (*recaka*), [one should place it] upon that lotus; and by means of retention (*kumbhaka*), having bound it with both the left and right hands, one should consecrate [the deity] at the top of the *liṅga* with a measure of four finger-breadths, using cow-horn [powder]. Again, one should sprinkle oil with the Heart-mantra, and unguent of *āmalaka* with the Armor-mantra.

Having smeared the *liṅga* and its pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), having sprinkled them with pure water... (l. 5) having sprinkled the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) with the five Brahmans and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), having consecrated [them] with the *Vyomavyāpinī* [mantra], and having offered incense, lamps, and the *arghya* offering; having smeared the *liṅga* and its pedestal with fragrant water mixed with curd, ghee, honey, the essence of sugarcane, the essence of fruits, coconut water, musk, camphor, and saffron by means of the *astra* [mantra]; and having filled [the vessel] with the *hṛdaya* [mantra]. (p. 21a, l. 1)

...having worshipped; having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, lamp, and water for honor (*arghya*); having sprinkled with water; having performed the thousand-stream consecration (*sahasradhārābhiṣeka*) and the bathing with the water from the nine jars (*navakalaśasnāna*); having sprinkled with the water from the conch using the five Brahmā-mantras; having placed a single flower upon the head;
[and] according to the *Siddhāntaratnākara*, [the application of] oil massage, flowers, *āmalaka* fruit, cow products (*gavya*), and so forth.
The milk of the deceased Dadhīci,
the fragrance of camphor, sugarcane, fruit,
and coconut; and the scent of fragrant streams as if for the bathing of Śaṅkha.
Having performed the cleansing with a washed cloth and the rubbing [of the body] according to the Vīra-tantra,
one becomes pure by means of the yoga-cloth.

One should not perform [the rite] with a wet cloth; rather, having first beheld the sun at the proper time, one should fashion the *liṅgadeha* according to the rules— devoid of [ordinary] characteristics— with garments, perfumes, flowers,
garlands, sacred threads, and so forth, as well as crowns, earrings, necklaces, and strings of pearls, using the primary material.
In the forenoon one should wear yellow garments, at midday red garments, and in the evening variegated garments;
however, for the half-watch period, one should perform the ritual ablution. In the absence of these, white garments should be used; one may wear them at all times.
The height of the *liṅga* should be measured as one [unit]; the first [part] is wrapped with cloth,
the second is joined with ornaments, and the third is adorned with flowers.

On the fourth [day], one should smear all the limbs with fragrant unguents. Having offered a flower with the *mūla-mantra*, one should worship [the deity] upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*) with the *manonmanī-mantra*. One should offer the mantra as the sacrificial oblation (*havis*). Having presented incense, lamps, and the water-offering (*arghya*), one should perform the worship of the surrounding deities (*āvaraṇapūjā*). Having worshipped the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) on the pedestal and displayed the gesture of salutation (*namaskāramudrā*), [one worships] Ajitā.
Below the *liṅga-pīṭha*, the wise one should worship the five [faces] in the center:
Īśāna on the head, Īśa in the northeast, and the Puruṣa face in the east.

One should worship Aghora... Vajra and likewise Vāmadeva in the north; Sadyojātamukha and Bhṛṅgin in the west. The Heart should be worshipped in the southeast, and the Head should be worshipped... in the [northeast].

One should worship the *śikhā* in the northwest (*vāyavyā*), and one should worship the *varman* in the northeast (*īśe*). One should place the location of the eyes in the center, and the weapon (*astra*) at the head in that direction.
Having placed the *hṛdaya* ending with "namaḥ," [one should likewise use] "*vauṣaṭ*" and "*huṃ*."
One should worship [the deity] above the head with the mantras ending in *vauṣaṭ*, *oṃ*, *huṃ*, and *phaṭ*.
Thus, having worshipped in this manner first, one should worship the second [deity] upon the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*).
"One should meditate on the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) according to the upper row; this is the vow.

One should worship the Lords of the Gaṇas (gaṇeśas) in the region of the throat as the third enclosure. According to the lower row, one should worship the Guardians of the Directions (digpālas) as the fourth enclosure."
...and one should worship [the deity] upon a stone with the fivefold rite.
Thus is described the facial expression and likewise the bodily pride (*dehāhaṅkṛti*).
One should worship Sadāśiva, Maheśvara, Rudra, and the Lords of Wisdom (*dhīśvaras*). (l. 3)
From the eastern face up to the northeast, and from the northeast onwards, there are five;
thus there are five faces and twenty-five bodies.
One should worship the Lord of the Gods, the Lord of Devas, as well as the downward-facing one, which is likewise remembered.
In this manner, [one worships] the head in sequence:
in the northeast quarter, *oṃ hoṃ īśānāya namaḥ*;
in the eastern quarter, *oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣavaktrāya namaḥ*.
To the south: *namaḥ* to the heart of Aghora. To the left:
*oṃ hiṃ*, *namaḥ* to the face of Vāmadeva. To the west: *oṃ haṃ*, *namaḥ* to the form of Sadyojāta. Having thus worshipped.
Aṃśumatī,
Gaurī, Gaṅgā, Gaṇāṛddhi, and Ambikā—
these five powers (pañcaśakti) one should worship in the directions starting from Īśāna.
In the southeast,
homage to the heart;
in the southwest, homage to the head.
In the northwest, *vauṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*);
in the northeast, *huṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*);
in the center, *vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes (*netratraya*).
In its northeast, one should worship with "Haḥ astrāya phaṭ. In the region of Maheśvara, [one says] "Namaḥ to the Vidyā-deha. In Sūkṣma and Vāminī in the southeast, and Nili in the domain of Nirṛti.
One should worship Cakri in the northeast (aniladeśa), Pāśāṅkī in the north (īśadeśaka),
Khaḍginī in the region of the head, and Gambhīrī in the range of the northwest (vāyugocara).
Then, one should worship Vāgīśvarī in the body of knowledge (vidyādeha) with a hundred prostrations.

In the second enclosure (*dvitīyāvaraṇa*): upon the upper fillet (*uparipaṭṭikā*) of the *viṭopa-ṭa*, one should worship Śakti in the eight directions beginning with the east. Having fully worshipped Ananta and the others, one should worship Śakti. [The eight Śaktis are] Śruti, Svadhā, Kṣānti, Ārti, Puṣṭi, Caturthikā, Śruti, Kīrti, Medhā, and Māyā—this is the group of eight. Having thus worshipped them in the region of the throat, one should worship two [deities] in each of the four directions beginning with the east. Having worshipped Indra and Īśāna, [one says]: "Obeisance to Nandin. (p. 23a, l. 1)

...In the center, obeisance to Mahākāla. Between Yama and Agni, obeisance to Bhṛṅgin. Between Yama and Nirṛti, obeisance to Gaṇapati. Between Nirṛti and Varuṇa, obeisance to Vṛṣabha. Between Vāyu and Varuṇa, obeisance to Skanda. Between Vāyu and Utkā, obeisance to Devī. Between Īśāna and Uttara, obeisance to Caṇḍeśvara. Having thus worshipped, one should worship the Śaktis: Kṛṣṇī, Icchā, Mālikā, Kaṇṭhī, Māhinī, Mālinī, as well as Nandī and Vanavallī—these are the eight Śaktis.

Thus they are to be worshipped. In the fourth enclosure (*caturthāvaraṇa*), having worshipped [the deities] from Indra to Viṣṇu on the lower frieze (*adhapaṭṭikā*) starting from the east, one should worship Śakti. [The ten Śaktis are: Śacī, Svāhā, Kālakaṇṭhī, Jātā, Hārīra, Mañjanā, Adhni, Jīvā, Arcadevī, and Śrī—these are the ten Śaktis. This is the fourth enclosure. Below, on the foundation stone (*ādhāraśilā*), having worshipped [the weapons] from the Vajra to the Cakra in the ten directions starting from the east, one should worship Śakti.
Vilāsirūpiṇī, Dhāruṇī, Vimukhatā,
Nirmalī, Durmali, Devīmati, Śruti, and Samālinī.
Sudarśana, Haṃsa, Malicā, [and] Śakti—
thus they are to be worshipped. This is the fifth enclosure in the Kāraṇa [mandala].
First, in the east, [the seats] of the limbs of Brahmā,
of the Vidyeśvaras, of the Gaṇeśvaras,
and of the ten weapons of the world-protectors.
From the sequence of the five non-obstructions of Īśvara.
Now, in the Brahma-section: from the east down to the bottom. The images are as follows: "Obeisance to the principle of Prakṛti," as previously stated. (l. 4)

Homage to the principle of the mind (*manas-tattva*). Homage to the principle of the intellect (*buddhi-tattva*). Homage to the principle of the ego (*ahaṃkāra-tattva*). Homage to the principle of power (*śakti-tattva*). Homage to the principle of the ear (*śrotra-tattva*). Homage to the principle of the skin (*tvak-tattva*). Homage to the principle of the eye (*cakṣus-tattva*). (l. 5) Homage to the principle of the tongue (*jihvā-tattva*). Homage to the principle of the nose (*ghrāṇa-tattva*). Homage to the principle of speech (*vāk-tattva*). Homage to the principle of the feet (*pāda-tattva*). Homage to the principle of the hands (*pāṇi-tattva*). Homage to the principle of the anus (*pāyu-tattva*). (l. 6) Homage to the principle of the generative organ (*upastha-tattva*). Homage to the principle of touch (*sparśa-tattva*).

Salutation to the principle of form (*rūpa-tattva*). Salutation to the principle of taste (*rasa-tattva*). Salutation to the principle of smell (*gandha-tattva*). Salutation to the principle of space (*ākāśa-tattva*). Salutation to the principle of wind (*vāyu-tattva*). Salutation to the principle of fire (*agni-tattva*). Salutation to the principle of the arts (*kalā-tattva*). Having thus worshipped, [one should recite]: *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the principle of the self (*ātma-tattva*). *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the Lord of the principle of the self, whose form is emanation (*sṛṣṭi-rūpa*). Salutation to Brahmā together with Sarasvatī. Having worshipped with the mantra "brahmajajñānam," etc.
Meditation [on] Brahmā, who has four faces, four arms, and hair rising upwards; who is endowed with a staff and a water-pot; ... *inspiring fear yet auspicious.* (l. 3)
Having meditated thus, one should worship Gāyatrī from the region of the throat down to the bottom of the upper fillet.

In the portion belonging to Viṣṇu, as before: *namaḥ* to the principle of extension (*yātatva*); *namaḥ* to the principle of the person (*puruṣatattva*); *namaḥ* to the principle of passion (*rāgatattva*); *namaḥ* to the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*); *namaḥ* to the principle of time (*kālatattva*); *namaḥ* to the principle of necessity (*niyatitattva*); *namaḥ* to the principle of space (*kālātattva*). Having worshipped thus, [one should recite]: *oṃ hāṃ vidyātattvāya namaḥ*. *Namaḥ* to the Lord of the principle of knowledge, whose form is stability; *namaḥ* to Mahālakṣmī-Viṣṇu. Having worshipped with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," [there follows] the meditation: "And his lotus-like face has the form known as blue."
I bow to that peaceful Vāsudeva, who wears yellow garments, whose hands grant boons and protection, who holds the discus as his weapon, and who bears a conch and a crown upon his head.
Having consecrated [it] with the mantra "That which was proclaimed at the beginning of the Veda as the vowels," one should perform the visualization.
Four-faced and eight-armed, endowed with twelve eyes,
[he holds] a skeleton, a drum (*ḍiṇḍima*), a noose, a bell, and incense;
he is equipped with hands in the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, and is resplendent with a sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*).

"Reddish in appearance, with sandals on the feet, and adorned with a crown of matted locks"—having thus consecrated the *gāyatrī*, one should worship in the region of Sadāśiva with: "Obeisance to the gross principle (*sthūlatattva*); obeisance to the subtle principle (*sūkṣmatattva*); obeisance to the principle of time (*kālatattva*). Thus one should worship.
Salutation to Sadāśiva, who is accompanied by Manonmanī in the form of grace.
Having consecrated [the object] with the mantra "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām," [one should perform] meditation.
With an appearance resembling the autumn moon, endowed with a lotus, possessed of ten arms, with one [face] at the heart and one at the throat,
having two feet, richly adorned with variegated garments, and decorated with all ornaments.
Adorned with a crown of matted hair and equipped with a chisel and a trident, he is likewise endowed with a sword and a vajra; in his right hands, he firmly holds the gesture of fearlessness,
a noose, the boon-granting gesture, a bell, fire, and a hook that burns.

Having meditated thus: "Held in the left hand... (p. 25a, l. 1), and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *Gāyatrī*, one proceeds from the upper band onwards in the portion belonging to Rudra, circling from the east to the east: "Obeisance to the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā-tattva*); obeisance to the principle of Īśvara; obeisance to the principle of Sadāśiva; obeisance to the principle of Śakti; obeisance to the principle of Śiva; obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the principle of Śiva; obeisance to Rudra accompanied by Rudrāṇī. Having consecrated [the object] with the mantra "yo rudro agnau" (He who is Rudra in the fire)...
He is absorbed in meditation, enriched by the quality of the fire of his eyes, with a serpent as his sacred thread;
his pair of hands and feet possess the color of wine, and his throat is like the fire of Time.
I bow to the one in the form of Rudra, who holds the gesture of granting fearlessness, a trident, a rosary, and fire in his left hands, and who bears a deer and possesses a white form.
Having meditated thus and performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *gāyatrī*, [one performs] the three triads of principles (*tritatva*).
Then, in the upper portion belonging to Maheśvara, one should worship the eight purifiers (*pūryaṣṭaka*):

"Salutation to the principle of ego (*ahaṅkāra-tattva*); salutation to the principle of mind (*manas-tattva*); salutation to the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*); salutation to the principle of smell (*gandha-tattva*)."
Salutation to the principle of taste. Salutation to the principle of form. Salutation to the principle of touch. Salutation to the principle of sound.
Having thus worshipped, [one should worship] Maheśvarī, who is accompanied by Mahe..., whose essential nature is concealment.
...having meditated upon the form of light in its center and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the Gāyatrī,
one should worship Maheśa as the Lord (*Īśvara*), the essence consisting of the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*), with the mantra joined [to it]. This brings about all auspicious success.

Thus, having worshipped the form of the Śivāsana, which is the limb of enjoyment (bhogāṅga); having worshipped the limbs of Brahmā, such as the three eyes and so forth, belonging to the Vidyā-deha; having performed the invocation (āvāhana); ...(l. 3)... having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the sequence of kalās beginning with the inner measure (antarmātrā) and so forth; having displayed the five mudrās beginning with the Deva-mudrā; and having offered incense and lamps.

Having performed the rites of *pādya* (water for the feet) and *ācamana* (water for sipping) with the *astra-mantra*, [one should perform] the *vija...* (l. 4)... the *daṇḍabhaṅgī* and the *layāṅga-ṇḍabhaṅgika*. One should worship all the *liṅgas* according to the sequence of worship that has been reached. Having worshipped the *naivedya* (food offering) and the *ambīma...* (l. 5)... one should place the vessel containing the food offerings along with its condiments upon the triple-footed stand (*tripādukā*). Having struck the bell with the *astra-mantra*, [one should offer it] to the *kāraṇa*, the *asuras*, the *rākṣasas*... (l. 6)... the *piśācas*, and the *brahmarākṣasas*. By the sound of the jewel-bell, they are driven away by that [offering]. Having presented the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) and betel at the door of Vighneśvara, afterwards [one should perform] the presence of the deity... (l. 7)...

One should worship the vessel with the Astra-mantra. Having performed the fivefold purification (*pañcaśuddhi*), one should place a flower in the center of the oblation (*havya*). Having displayed the Mahāmudrās, such as the Dhenu-mudrā and others, one should render it nectar-like (*amṛtīkṛta*) with the Kavaca-mantra. Having sprinkled it with the Bhogāṅga-mantra, and having poured water around it, one should prepare the meal. Having recited the *Annasūkta* with the mantra "Prāṇāya svāhā," and having offered it while circumambulating with one's own hand, one should contemplate that it has been given.

Having joined the food with the hand of Prakṛti for the purpose of offering it into the hand of Śiva, and having given the *uttarāpośana* (the concluding water for the meal), one should set aside the cooking vessel in another place. Having poured pure water three times for the purpose of washing the hands, mouth, and feet...
[one should offer] rice mixed with jaggery (*gulānna*) into the upward-facing mouth;
rice with sesame seeds (*tilānna*) into the eastern-facing mouth; and likewise rice with mung beans (*mudgānna*) into the southern-facing mouth.
In the west, one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasānna*) to the five-faced [deity]... (l. 6).
As long as there is fruit and essence, even the eating of a wild boar;
one should act in such a way that what has been eaten is offered to the face of the *liṅga*.
The sipping of water (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and the water for the feet (*pādya*) are performed with one, five, and [five] counts respectively.

(p. 26b l. 1) Regarding the worship of the Goddess (*devīpūjā*): having placed [the offerings] upon her hands and head, and upon her feet, one should present mouth-perfume (*mukhavāsa*) for the purpose of cleansing the mouth. Having offered *tāmbūla* together with cardamom, cloves, camphor, and small pills (l. 2), one should worship the infinite seat (*anantāsana*) for the sake of the ritual services (*upacāra*). Having displayed [the offerings] with the five faces and limbs according to the sequence of mantras for incense, lamps, and so forth (l. 3), one should dismiss [the deity] and wash one’s hands.

Having performed the ritual services (*upacāra*) in due order—beginning with the night-offering (*rātrikā*), collyrium, ash, mirror, umbrella, chowrie, fan, betel, and covering—and having offered the *arghya*, *ācamanīya*, mantra-flowers, and benedictions; thereafter, having recited the study of the four Vedas, the *sūtras*, various hymns (*stotra*), proclamations, songs, and so forth in sequence; and having [performed] the services of rhythmic clapping, instrumental music, singing, and dancing in the dance pavilion (*nṛttamaṇṭapa*)—[one should] inform [the deity]. Thus is the procedure for the worship of Śiva.

Then, in the northern part of the main pavilion, one should invoke the seat, the image, and so forth with the *umā*-mantra and the root mantra (*mūla*). Having displayed the five-faced mudrās beginning with *sthāpana*, one should perform the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the twenty-five *kalās* of the *mātrikās*. For the sake of consecration, one should sprinkle [the deity] with water from the *arghya* vessel using the root mantra of Śakti. Having removed the [old] garment, one should perform the rubbing with another cloth, adorn [the deity] with garments, perfumes, garlands, and so forth, and clothe [it] with golden ornaments, necklaces, and the like. Having worshipped the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), one should invoke [the deity] and empower it ten times with the *gāyatrī* and the heart mantra (*hṛdaya*). [The following is] the meditation (*dhyāna*).
Dark-complexioned, wearing variegated garments, with a lotus-like face, her limbs adorned with gold;

her hair bound up, posed in the triple-bend (*tribhaṅgi*), graced by the fullness of her breasts, [she whose] feet are turned downwards, possessing the limbs of yoga, the power of the [divine] portions;
holding a white water-lily in her left hand, with arms extended.
"O Goddess, whose eyes are victorious and supreme... homage to you, O Goddess of gods.
Having meditated thus, one should worship [her] together with the Śaktis, using the Brahmā-aṅgas beginning with Īśāna, in the second enclosure.

In the eight directions beginning with the east, one should worship [the goddesses] starting from Vāmā and ending with Sarvabhūtadamani. In the center, one should fully worship Maheśvarī. In the enclosure of the seats, in the eight directions beginning with the east, one should worship the Śaktis of Indra and the others. To the south is Śānī; to the left of Nirṛti is Sarasvatī; and Mahālakṣmī is to be worshipped. Having offered the food offering, incense, lamp, and water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), one should thus perform the worship of the Śaktis of enjoyment. This is the procedure for the daily oblation (*nityahoma*).

In the sacrificial pavilion in the northeast, or in the kitchen, one should prepare a square or circular fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one *hasta* in width, provided with three tiers (*mekhalā*). Having visualized the self as the face of the deity, facing either east or north, one should fashion the navel above the upper tier. Sitting upon the seat facing the region of the navel, having performed the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and other rites of ritual purification (*sakalīkaraṇa*), with hands holding the sacred grass (*pavitra*), and having placed the general offering water (*sāmānyārghya*) with the syllable *praṇava*, one should sprinkle the fire-pit with that offering water.

Having smeared that site with cow dung using the *kṣetra-mantra*, having performed the cleansing (*mārjana*), and having purified the materials placed to the right with the *astra-mantra* through the five-fold purification (*pañca-śuddhi*), one should adorn it with the five powders (*pañca-cūrṇa*). Then, the procedure for the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) consisting of the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) is shown.

In the south, west, north, and center, the *kalās* should be worshipped. Having encircled [the area] with a triple-thread using the *astra-mantra*, one should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Ananta, and the others. With hands holding *darbha* grass, one should perform the drawing... [known as] *ullekhana*. Within the drawn [space], the four-footed [deity] should be worshipped with the *astra-mantra*. In the center, north, and south, the presiding deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra should be worshipped. On the other line, one should worship him who stands in the *raudra* [state]. In the middle of that—

Having placed the four-footed [diagram] and the half-hook with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) during the previously mentioned night, and having established the protection-cloth upon *darbha* grass with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), one should worship Vāgīśī and Vāgīśvara above the central circle with perfumes and other offerings. Having placed the fire from the kitchen in an earthen vessel or a copper vessel, and having deposited it on the left side of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should worship it with the root-mantra (*mūla*).

Then, one should emit the fire—the elemental fire (*bhūtāgni*)—from the center through the path of the *suṣumnā* channel into the end of the *kumbha* by means of exhalation (*recaka*). Having joined it with the *baṃdhava* fire and worshipped it, one should contemplate the fire as Śiva. One should worship it with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*). Having placed another fire into the fire-vessel (*agnipātra*), one should cast away the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyād*), the fragment of fire, toward the region of Nirṛti. In the middle of the fire, one should worship the *saṃhitā* beginning with the three principles (*tatva-traya*). One should invoke [the deity] with the root mantra; its form is as follows.
Having placed the fire-vessel above the navel, one should visualize Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara upon the *kūrca* grass, possessing youthful forms. The meditation [is as follows]:
[She has] a dark-colored body... [She is] very youthful, her head adorned with a garland of *soma* and her hair [adorned]. (l. 2)
"I meditate upon the nectar of the face of Pūrṇasoma, O Mother of the Supreme Fire...
(l. 3). Having meditated thus, one should worship with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī. Then, having worshipped Vāgīśvara in her vicinity, [one should perform] the meditation (*dhyāna*).

Having meditated thus: "The Lord Vāgīśvara, three-eyed, white in color, four-armed, holding the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus," [one should recite]: *oṃ hāṃ vāgīśvarāya namaḥ*. Then, having circled the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the *samhitā* mantra, [one should place] the fire at the tip of the nose with both hands raised above one's own knees, which rest upon the ground, while reciting the root mantra.

One should join [it] by way of the *yoni*. Having placed the vessel at the region of the navel of the *kuṇḍa*, having sprinkled it with water, and having deposited a flower, [one should perform] up to the end of the flower...

Having placed [the fire] in another location, one should deposit a *ḍalabindu* with the *hṛdaya[-mantra]* for the sake of purification, ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), and cleansing; having covered it with dry fuel using the *varma[-mantra]*, one should kindle it with the *astra[-mantra]*. Having worshipped the embryonic fire (*garbhāgni*) on all sides, one should consecrate it with the *astra[-mantra]* for the protection of the embryo, and bind a *darbha*-grass bracelet on both wrists with the *kavaca[-mantra]*. One should worship [the fire] with the *sadyojāta[-mantra]* for the purpose of the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*). Then, having offered three oblations of sesame seeds with the *hṛdaya[-mantra]*, one should perform the *homa* with sesame seeds.

In the third month, for the sake of the *pumsavana* rite, having worshipped with the *Vāmadeva* mantra, one should offer three oblations of sesame seeds into the head [of the fire], and having cast a drop of water from the left hand, in the sixth month, for the sake of the *sīmantonnayana* rite, having propitiated with the *Aghora* mantra and offered three oblations of sesame seeds with the *Vāma* mantra, one should consecrate it three times with that same mantra for the purpose of fashioning the face and limbs as before; and in the tenth month, for the sake of birth, one should worship with the *Puruṣa* mantra.

Having offered three oblations of sesame seeds with the *kavaca* mantra, one should meditate upon the fire-born [deity]. For the purpose of bathing after the impurity of childbirth, [one should use] the tips of darbha grass from the fire...

...having removed the previous bracelet from the hand of the Goddess with the *mūla-mantra*; having tied a golden bracelet on the hand of the Goddess for the protection of the child; having worshipped [the deity] with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*); having sprinkled the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) for the sake of purification after birth (*sūtaka-śauca*); having struck it with *darbha* grass; having sprinkled it with the armor-mantra (*varman*); for the sake of protecting the fire, having placed the encircling grass-belt (*paristharaṇa*) starting from the east with *darbha* grass upon the girdle; and having established the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) in the four directions with the weapon-mantra.

Having joined the five fuel-sticks (*samidh*) together at their roots and tips, and having offered them into the fire with the *svāhā* mantra while meditating on the meaning of the mantras, one should worship the forms of Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Ananta in the four directions starting from the east, at the locations of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). Having placed two fuel-sticks above and below with the *astra-mantra* for the sake of protection in the eastern direction and so forth, one should worship in sequence in the eight directions ending with Īśāna, saying "Obeisance to Indra" and so on. One should worship Brahmā and Viṣṇu as previously described.
One should contemplate the fire as the *bālāgni*.
Meditation:
having the color of a child’s fire,
with six eyes, two faces, and seven tongues.

Having taken up the *sruva* ladle, the *sruc* vessel, the fan, and the bell—[the implements] known as the *śāla*, *akara*, and *temara*—and having worshipped the "Child Fire" (*bālāgni*) with the mantra:

*oṃ hāṃ bālāgnaye namaḥ*, one should grasp the *sruva* and *sruc* with their faces turned upward and downward respectively. Having performed the five purifications (*pañcaśuddhi*), one should touch the roots, middles, and tips of the *darbha* grass with the root, middle, and tip of the *sruva* and *sruc* [respectively], thereby consecrating Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra. Having whirled them around the fire and cast the *darbha* blades into the fire, one should consecrate the respective deities at those specific locations, from the base to the top, using their respective root mantras.
...having placed [the vessel] upon *kuśa* grass in that portion; having worshipped Śiva and Śakti upon those two; having encircled it with a three-stranded thread while reciting the *kavaca* mantra;
[then] the meditation:
...the auspicious *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are Śakti.
The hollow of the two openings is the form of the essence of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).

The tip is the sound at the end of sound (*nādāntanāda*), the state consisting of nectar, the root of food and the eater of food. United... it is purified by mantra, the sleep of the sun, moon, and other [elements] within the throat.
The primordial reality of the center, possessing a beautiful luster produced by the stalks of the lotus and the moon, is beginningless.

Having meditated thus: (l. 2) having placed [the vessel] upon the upper girdle on the left side of the cow-product...; having filled it with clarified butter (*ājya*); having performed the purification as before; slightly to the southeast near the navel; having ignited a *darbha*-fire at the front for the sake of purification; having swirled the clarified butter; having cast it into the fire; having sprinkled two tips of *darbha* grass with the clarified butter using the *astra-mantra*; having placed the clarified-butter vessel above the navel; one should unite the fire. Thereafter:

Having meditated upon one’s own self as consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, [one should perform] the over-stepping (*atidhāvana*) and the over-hearing (*atiśravaṇa*) with the respective mantras. Having established the *arghya* water in the south-eastern direction (*īśānabhāga*) with *darbha*-blades, one should offer an oblation (*juhuyāt*) with the tip of a *kuśa* blade. Having cast into the midst of the clarified butter (*ājya*) a *pavitraka* made of two *darbha* blades, a span (*prādeśa*) in length, with a knot in the middle, one should [recite] the *Hṛdaya[-mantra]*.

...the sprinkling [is performed] with the left and right little fingers and thumbs, having grasped the tips and the bases equally and performed the sprinkling three times. In the city [of the fire], the sprinkling is as before. Having untied the knot of that purifier (*pavitra*) with the *astra* mantra, and having thoroughly sprinkled it with the *arghya* water, one should cast it into the fire. For the purpose of making the purifiers, having kindled them with single blades of *darbha* grass, and having displayed the vessels containing the clarified butter and sacrificial materials, one should whirl them around the fire and cast them away.

Again, having purified the sacrificial ladle with darbha grass and prepared the clarified butter (*ājya*), one should take hold of the triad of *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā* on the southern side of the butter. Saying "Svāhā to Agni," one takes the clarified butter from the south-eastern portion; saying "Oṃ Hāṃ, Svāhā to Soma," [one offers it] to the left eye of the Fire-god. Taking [the butter] from the middle portion, [one says] "Oṃ Hāṃ, [Svāhā] to Agni and Soma."

Having offered with "Svāhā" into the middle eye of Agni; and with "Oṃ hāṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā" into the mouth of Agni; and having offered with "Svāhā" into the [mouth of] Śiva—[then], during the dark fortnight: "Oṃ hāṃ somāya svāhā. ... Having taken clarified butter from the left side into the left eye of Agni with "Oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā"; having taken [butter] from the middle into the right eye of Agni with "Oṃ hāṃ somāgnibhyāṃ svāhā";
and having offered as before with "Oṃ hāṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā" into the mouth of Agni with "Svāhā," one should mix the remainder of the fire-oblation with other clarified butter.

Thus, having performed the purification of the clarified butter (*ājya*) during the bright and dark fortnights, one should again consecrate it with the *saṃhitā* [mantra], perform the binding and the sprinkling (*avakuṇṭhana*), transform it into nectar by means of the *surabhi-mudrā*, and consecrate it with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*). Then, by scattering drops of clarified butter while reciting the heart mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*), one should worship Vighneśa. Following that: *oṃ haṃ sadyojātāya svāhā*; *oṃ hiṃ vāmadevāya svāhā*; *oṃ huṃ aghorāya svāhā*;
[and] with the heart mantra... (p.32a, l.1).

Having offered one oblation with the mantra: *oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣavaktrāya svāhā | oṃ hoṃ īśānāya svāhā*, and having offered [oblations] through the mouth of the fire (*agnimukha*) for Aghora... [with the mantras: *oṃ haṃ hiṃ sadyojātavāmadevābhyāṃ svāhā | oṃ hiṃ huṃ vāmadevāghorābhyāṃ svāhā | oṃ huṃ heṃ aghoratatpuruṣābhyāṃ svāhā | oṃ heṃ hoṃ tatpuruṣeśānābhyāṃ svāhā*, one should perform the conjunction of the faces (*mukhasaṃyoga*).

For the purpose of unifying the sacrificial fire (*makha-ekikaraṇa*), one should offer oblations with the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles, beginning from the southeast (*āgneya*) to the northwest (*vāyavya*), and from the southwest (*naiṛtya*) to the northeast (*īśāna*), saying "Svāhā," while worshipping up to the Lord of the Directions (*saddīśānta*). This constitutes the unification of the faces (*vaktra-ekikaraṇa*). For the purpose of naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), one should worship with the *Īśāna* mantra. Having offered three oblations with the *astra* mantra, one should assign the name "Hutāśana" to the fire residing in Śiva. Then, having worshipped the fire along with its parents within the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), ending with the word "namaḥ," one should honor it with flowers. For the purpose of joining the tongues (*jihvā-sandhāna*), [one should worship] twice in the middle of the fire, starting from the east and the south...

...having offered *darbha* grass into the fire; having held the vessel of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *sruva* spoon; having offered an oblation (*āhuti*) with the root mantra and performed the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*); having shown the gesture of salutation (*añjalimudrā*) as a prostration to Agni; (l. 2) having presented incense, lamps, and the water offering (*arghya*); having secured the protection (*rakṣā*) over the cooking pot (*sthālī*); having taken a flower with the root mantra of the form of Agni (*agnimūrtti*); having applied the protection; having approached the presence of the deity accompanied by those performing the services and chanting auspicious sounds (*svasti*); (l. 3) having performed the offering of a handful of flowers (*mantrapuṣpāñjali*).

Having performed the protection rite (*rakṣā*) upon the head of the deity, having offered incense, lamps, and water for honor (*arghya*) with the Brahma-mantras and their limbs (*aṅga*), and having established that very Lord of All (*Sarveśvara*), one should perform the protection rite together with the gods (*bhūsura*) upon one's own forehead. This is the procedure for the daily fire-ritual (*nityāgnividhi*).
[Now follows] the procedure for the festival of the Goddess (*devyotsavavidhi*).

The preceptor, together with his attendants, desiring to perform the ritual offering (*bali*), having approached the presence [of the deity], having sprinkled [the materials] with the general *arghya* water using the *astra-mantra*, having performed worship, having arranged the vehicle [of the deity], having displayed the mudrās beginning with the installation (*sthāpana*), having offered incense, lamps, and *arghya*, and having performed the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with garments, perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and so forth.

...having placed [the syllables] in the *paka*, having bound it firmly, and having worshipped the seat (*āsana*) and so forth as before, one should invoke [the deity]. Having honored the *Gāyatrī* and having placed the *mātṛkā-kalā* and other elements, one should meditate on the Śakti as before:
four-armed, three-eyed, adorned with a crown of matted hair, holding a deer in the left hand and an axe and a shield in the right.
Beautiful in every limb, [clad in] a tiger-skin upper garment,
with Umā on his left, possessing three eyes, adorned with a crown of skulls, the goddess holding a lotus in her right hand, in the *tribhaṅgī* posture, and [adorned] with other ornaments...
Having meditated [on her], one should worship the goddesses beginning with Mīśāna with the six limbs;
this is the second enclosure (*dvitīyāvaraṇa*). One should worship the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*); in the third enclosure, the world-protectors (*lokapāla*).

Having fully worshipped the goddess Gaurī, and having offered food-offerings (*naivedya*), incense, lamps, and water for honor (*arghya*), one should again adorn her with garments, garlands, and so forth.

Having placed the deity upon [the throne] with parasols, whisks, fans, incense, lamps, and all the offerings of musical instruments along with the attendants, and having offered the *huṃ* into the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*), [one prepares] the vessel for the master’s consecration (*ācāryābhiṣeka*).

...in the regions of the south-east, north-east, and south-west. Having offered oblations beginning with *hiraṇya* and ending with *rūpa*, as before, in the sequence of union with the mouth, having offered oblations from *oṃ ṣūṃ* up to the end of *ha*, one should meditate upon the unification of the three tongues. [Performing] the rites beginning with the consumption of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) for the Lord of Sacrifice and ending with the marriage ceremony... thereafter, for the sake of that rite, having offered three oblations for each using the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*), [one prepares] a large sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with a mouth of the desired dimensions... [saṅkalpa...]

Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* as prescribed with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* upon the tongue, using the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, one should cast into the fire clarified butter (*ājya*) in the measure of a barley grain from the *sruk*—thus having performed the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should sit down. Having sprinkled water around the fire (*pariṣeka*) and worshipped it with the root mantra and the *saṃhitā* mantras, one should meditate on [the deity] in the sacrificial fire. One should offer oblations extending sixteen finger-breadths to the edge of one's own seat. Then, having worshipped the seat again and displayed the external *āpūrvā* mudrā, [one should worship] the fire...
To be honored. Meditation.
He has tawny limbs and three eyes, adorned with a crown of matted hair;
he holds a rosary on his right side, while on the left he carries a sacrificial ladle (*sruk*), a sacrificial spoon (*sruva*), and a lance (*tomara*);
he is mounted upon a bull and wears a white sacred thread.
