O God, you are clothed in a tiger skin, eternally maintaining the sacred fire, and possessing the form of an old man.

Having meditated thus and worshipped Varuṇa, having offered oblations of the three principles (*tatva*) and the three [other] principles beginning with the *vyāpaka-āvaraṇa*, having sprinkled water around the fire, and having offered sixteen-fold oblations of clarified butter and other substances together with the root mantra, having offered three oblations with the *astra-mantra* for the sake of expiation, having offered the *paṃpātā* oblation, and having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* with the words "To the Vasus, to the Rudras," and so forth, one should worship the deities of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).

Having gathered the *aghora* fuel-sticks and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), and having cast them into the fire; having worshipped Indra and the other deities; having offered the inner and outer oblations (*antarbali* and *bahirbali*) at the petals; having dismissed the deities; having sprinkled water around the fire; having gathered the surrounding grass (*paristaraṇa*); and having sprinkled [the area] with the *arghya* water; having gathered the remains of the ointment (*lepa*). (p. 34b, l. 1)

The attendant, together with the oblation vessel (*havisthālī*), should strike the bell with the syllables *śrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ* according to their respective measures (*mātrā*). Accompanied by words expressing "well-being" (*svasti*) and "salutation" (*namaḥ*), he should scatter water at the eastern, southern, northern, and middle points of the door. Having placed a flower above that [door], he should protect it, perform the concealment (*avakuṇṭhana*), and display the divine mudrā. Regarding the fruits: the best is the *sū...purāṇḍa*, the middling is the *likuca* fruit, and the lowest is the *āmalaka*.

In the gathering, for the deities it is five-fingered and circular; for the *bhūtas* it is long; for the *śaktis* it is triangular; for the sages (*munis*) it is like a mountain; for the *yakṣas* it is merely a fist; [for the *piśācas*] it is the shape of a cart; for the *paiśācas* it is the form of a spear; for humans, having held [the hand] with the fingers joined, the measure of the offering (*balimāna*) is prescribed. Having thus taken [it], [one recites]: *oṃ hāṃ...nāya svāhā*. *oṃ hāṃ vighneśvarāya svāhā*.
Having offered the oblation with "Oṃ hāṃ vighnarājāya svāhā," [he offers] to the south: "Oṃ hāṃ daṇḍine svāhā"; to the north: "Oṃ hāṃ muṇḍine svāhā."

At the front of the bull: *oṃ hāṃ vṛṣābhāya svāhā*. On its back: *saṃvarttabhūtāya svāhā*. Having offered thus, [offer]: *samāvarttabhūtāya svāhā*. To the south: *kuṇḍodarabhūtāya svāhā*. To the south of that: *brahmāṇyā devyai svāhā*, and likewise *caṇḍikādevyai svāhā*. Having offered the *bali* offering up to this point, offer the *bali* to the east and west of it with: *vīrabhadravighneśvarābhyāṃ svāhā*.

In the southwest, [to] Dīrgha... (l. 4) ...and to the west of that, *mahāgaṇapataye svāhā*. To the short [deity] of the celestial chariot (*vimāna*)... *svāhā*. In the northwest, to the one who has become a lion-form (*siṃharūpabhūtāyai*)... (l. 5) ...and to the west of that, *guhabhūtāya svāhā*. To its east: *oṃ hāṃ jyeṣṭhāyai svāhā*. To the south: *oṃ hāṃ gajamukhyai svāhā*. ...(l. 6) To the south of that: *oṃ hāṃ durgāyai svāhā*. To the east of that: *oṃ hāṃ sūryāya svāhā*. In the northeast, *brahmaṇe svāhā*. Having thus offered the oblation (*bali*), (p. 35b, l. 1).

In the second enclosure, to the south and north of its gate: *oṃ hāṃ amodāya svāhā | oṃ pramodāya svāhā*. At the front of the second bull, as before... at the back, *indrāya svāhā*—thus the offering of strength (*balasama*). Incense, lamps, sacred learning, wisdom, song, rhythm, drums, dance, singing, instrumental music, and so forth should be announced. Having offered the final oblation (*balinda*), to the south of that [gate], [one offers] *kṣetrapālāya svāhā*.

For the sake of the third enclosure, having again offered [oblations] three times in the enclosure—at the Nairṛta [corner] ... *svāhā*, and at the Īśāna [corner] to Brahmā *svāhā*—and having thus given [the offerings], [one proceeds] to the eastern region of the *bhūtapīṭha*. Having washed the pedestal (*beripīṭha*) facing north, [one places] the *kumuda* [pedestal] upon it. Having worshipped the deities beginning with Indra in the eight directions, [one places] the cloth (*paṭikā*) upon that. ... in the northern direction. *Namaḥ* to Brahmā. Between Brahmā and Īśāna, *namaḥ* to the Ādityas.
Between Īśāna and Indra, *namaḥ* to the Rudras. (p. 36a, l. 1)

Salutation to Kṣetrapāla. Salutation to Indra. Between Indra and Agni, salutation to the hosts of Apsarases. Between Vāyu and Soma... [lacuna] ...between Soma and Īśāna, salutation to the Rudras. Thus they are to be worshipped. Outside the pedestal, in the east, salutation to the hosts of Piśācas; in the south, salutation to the Gaṇas; in the west, salutation to the Rākṣasas; in the north, salutation to the Gandharvas; in the northeast, salutation to the Bhūtas. Thus they are to be fully honored.

Having worshipped the eight [deities] on the upper petals... (l. 4)... [they] should be fully honored. In the center of the pericarp: *Oṃ hāṃ avighnāya namaḥ*. On the eastern petal: *pramodāya namaḥ*. On the southern [petal]: *pramodāya namaḥ*. (l. 5) On the western petal: *pramukhāya namaḥ*. On the northern petal: *vimukhāya namaḥ*. On the northeastern petal: *vighnahantre namaḥ*. Thus they should be worshipped. Having thus offered [the mantra] *namo... svāhā* to the deities, (l. 6) and having given the *bali* offering with that [mantra], one should give a food *bali* in the center the size of a coconut. Having offered incense, lamps, and the *arghya* water, one should announce all the ritual services (*upacāra*). Again... (p. 36b, l. 1).

Having worshipped the Deity and performed the adoration of the sandals (*pādukārcana*), thus concludes the procedure for the *balidāna* offering. On the secondary pedestal (*upapīṭha*) is the vow of the eight Nāgas, the two Dvāyus, and the Gaṇas. Kumuda... (l. 2)... the five [Nāgas]. The sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is for all the Rākṣasas. It is said that the horizontal band (*paṭṭikā*) is above, and the Kinnara... the Lord of the Gaṇas (*Gaṇeśvara*). Above that, it is said, is the station (*pada*) known as the Hundred Rudras (*Śatarudra*)... (l. 3). With five faces, four-fold symmetry, and eyes on his forehead; ten ears, ten arms, ten tridents, and ten [objects] held;
with one throat and one heart, his complexion is exceedingly red. (l. 4)
The form of the *balipīṭha* consists of two feet and the word *mitibhūta*.
Āmoda, Pramoda, Apramukha, Vimukha, Avighna, and Vighnakartṛ—these six are the leaders of the *bali* offerings. (l. 5)
For the Bhavādis, however, it is a *devikā*;

for Indra and the others, it is human; for the Bhūtādis, it is self-arisen (*svayambhūti*); in the eighth, however, it is the surrounding retinue (*parivāraka*). For Bāṇa and the others, it is among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas.
Ananta and the others reside in the divine liṅga; Bali resides in the seven-liṅga.
...Bali... Śarva, Tathā, Īśāna, Pāśupata, and Ugra as well.

...is remembered as the eightfold form (aṣṭamūrtti). [There is] the human liṅga... [and] the *bhūliṅga* offering. The supreme [liṅga] is in the eastern quarter; the four-faced one is in the southeast.
Kuṇḍodara is in the south, and [the liṅga] that pierces [obstacles] is in the southwest...
In the northwest [varūṇī] is the lion-faced one, and in the north-west [vāyavyā] is the downward-facing one;
in the north [soma] is the one-legged one, and in the northeast [aiśānī] is the eight-legged one... (l.4)...one should offer the bali-oblation to the retinue of the eight bhūtas.
Āṣāḍha, Liṅga,
Bali, Vṛṣa, Caṇḍin, Dhara, Śukra, Vahni, Brahmā, the group of Śaktis,
Gaṇapa, Jyeṣṭhā, Durgā, Dharaṇī, and Jayanta.
Śrīṇi, Nīlarudra, Bāṇaliṅga, Bali, Yatho, Dhruva, Pañca,
Agnilocana, Pratyuṣa, and Prabhāva— these are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
[This is] the Rākṣasaliṅga-bali.
Rākṣasas, paiśācas, asiddhas, vidyādharas, as well as kinnaras and kiṃpuruṣas— all these are proclaimed to be siddhas.
The offering to the divine liṅgas:
Ananteśa, as well as Sūkṣma,
Santatana, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śrikhaṇḍika.
One should perform the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*), the fire sacrifice (*homa*), and the worship of the retinue (*parivārārcana*)...
three times [a day], or at the time of sunrise, or at the junctures of time; this is the measure for the offering (*bali*).

The best [quantity] is said to be a *bāhula*; the middling is a *muṣṭhi*... the lowest is said to be a *svā...*—thus is the *bali* described. Now follows the propitiation of the sandals (*pādukārādhana*).

Having placed [it] upon a vessel, one should worship it. ... Having adorned it with garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments beginning with [the letter] *la*, one should fully worship the sandals (*pādukā*) with its own mantra and the mantra of the bull (*vṛṣabha*). One should protect it, encircle it (*avakuṇṭhya*), and display the great mudrā of the iron-linga (*ayorasa-liṅga-mahāmudrā*).
The meditation (*dhyāna*):
[He is] resembling the pomegranate flower, with hair standing erect and three eyes.
The supreme deity, holding a noose and a goad,
adorned with a garland of white *arkī* flowers, wearing yellow garments.
Having meditated on what is called the "form of the sandals," one should contemplate the deity.

Having thus meditated, [the deity] is to be worshipped. ...Having offered food, incense, lamps, and the water-offering (*arghya*), and having placed [the sandals] upon the head of the attendant, [one should perform] the ritual service with all musical instruments together with the deity. ...[The deity] ...with flowers, one should release the handful of water while reciting the mantra: Oṃ hāṃ! O protector of the secret and so forth, please accept this rite performed by us. May there be success for me through you, who abide by your own grace.
Oṃ hāṃ! Whatever action has been performed by me, whether good or evil, O Śiva, the bestower of fearlessness, may you consume that [karma] so that I may attain the state of Śiva.
Oṃ hāṃ! Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer; Śiva is this entire world.
Śiva performs sacrifice everywhere; he who is Śiva, may he indeed be I.

One should present the water for the guest-offering (*arghyodaka*) into the left hand of Śiva; and one should present oneself and the recitation (*japa*) into the right hand of the ritual expert (*karmadakṣa*).
Likewise, a certain specific detail regarding the cause has been stated:
having formed the añjali with the right hand, with the four fingers slightly contracted,
as if grasping a flower, one should offer the *vāstubali*.
At the conclusion of the worship, that which is designated as "water from the hollowed palms" (culukodaka) arises.
O Lord, Sovereign of the Entire World, until the conclusion of the worship with red lac,
may you remain present within this *liṅga* with the thought, "I am here."

Having thus made the request with the mantra, one should say "O God, forgive me" with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) while offering eight flowers. Having worshipped with the root mantra upon the vessel (*sthālī*), [one should worship] the flower-liṅga in the morning, the food-liṅga at midday, and the unbroken-rice (*akṣata*) liṅga in the evening.
... she is to be worshipped. Having offered the invocation and so forth, including the food offering, incense, lamp, and water for the guest, one should perform the meditation:
[She is] four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with a crown of matted hair. (l. 6)
O deer-eyed one... [it is] joined with the gesture of fearlessness and endowed with the gesture of granting boons.

Having meditated thus: "Adorned with a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and white garlands," the *Saṃhitā* should be worshipped. Having placed a vessel (*sthālikā*) upon the head of the pure Śaiva, [the worship] proceeds by means of the subsequent sequence, beginning with the previous water for the feet (*pādya*).
...having joined Maṇḍeśa, the Lord of Bulls, who is not obstructed by the *nāḍīs*, one should join him with water at midday.

Furthermore, having performed the pure dance (*śuddhanṛtta*) as described by Bharata in the *Pravṛtti*, and having duly performed the circumambulation, salutations, and recitation of mantras for the various Śiva-deities; having worshipped the Liṅga-deity with flowers as before and offered the *arghya*; and having caused the curtain to be drawn over the deity who is the form of Śiva for the Preceptor, one should go outside, perform the worship of Caṇḍa, and bring the floral remains (*nirmālya*) from Caṇḍeśvara.

Having established these [previously mentioned items] and consecrated the image of Caṇḍa with pure water, one should say: *oṃ hāṃ dhvaniścaṇḍāsanāya namaḥ*. Then, having worshipped the power of will (*icchāśakti*), one should invoke [the deity]. The rites of installation (*stāpana*) and so forth are as previously described. Having displayed the mudrās, performed the consecration, and adorned [the deity] with garments, perfumes, garlands of flowers, and other offerings, one should worship [it].
[Then follows] meditation (*dhyāna*).
And he has two colors and is adorned with a crown of matted locks;
an axe is in his right hand, while [a staff] is in his left hand at the level of the thigh.
With his right foot extended and his left foot lying down,
he wears the sacrificial thread and ornaments, and possesses the great splendor of Caṇḍeśa.
Having meditated thus: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍeśvara; huṃ phaṭ, obeisance," one should worship him.
Having worshipped his limbs, one should offer the remains of the deity's food and drink, betel, the offering of food (*naivedya*), incense, lamps, and water for honor (*arghya*).
This is for the sake of all ritual services (*upacāra*).
By the command of Śiva, may those who have attained great liberation through meditation on Caṇḍeśvara offer you the remains of their sacrificial offerings.

Having thus requested permission and offered the *arghya* with the root mantra (*mūla*), one should again perform obeisance at the heart with "HŪM PHAṬ SVĀHĀ" using the root mantra. Having offered the *arghya* turned away [from oneself], one should dismiss [the deity]. Then, having performed the eightfold hymn (*aṣṭaka-stotra*), obeisance, and so forth, one should perform recitation (*japa*) with the root mantra according to one's capacity. With the mind focused on the sound of the recitation, [one should pray]: "O Śambhu, grant the fruit of worship; O Caṇḍeśvara, obeisance to you. Having thus performed the ritual of the *kārasphoṭya*, this is the procedure for the worship of Caṇḍa.
Having risen early in the morning, and having meditated upon one's own guru, Gaṇeśa, and Śiva, one should perform the root-verse recitation (*mūlārjina*) and the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*).

...having performed the salutation... having washed the feet; having sipped water (ācamana); having entered the temple with the thought "I am Manonmanī"; standing near the door facing north on a beautiful seat... having performed the three watches [of the night] and having performed the *karanyāsa* (hand-assignment), as follows: "Oṃ hāṃ, phaṭ to the weapon"—having thus purified the back [of the hands] with the weapon-mantra... having flooded [the body] with the *śakti*-mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Manonmanī; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Manonmanī."

Placing the thumb upon the two little fingers... [thumb]... with the two index fingers: *oṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*. With the little and ring fingers: *namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ śirase namaḥ*. *Oṃ hūṃ śivāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ haiṃ kavacāyai namaḥ*. With the middle fingers on the palms of both hands: *oṃ hauṃ netrebhyo namaḥ*. With the two index fingers: *oṃ haḥ astrāya namaḥ*. Having thus performed the placement (*vinyāsa*), one should enclose [the deity] with the armor (*kavaca*), join [the hands], and place the form (*mūrti*) as the seat within the heart.
Beginning with the right thumb and little finger... (p. 40b, l. 1).

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart-mantra upon the heart, the head-mantra upon the head, the crest-mantra upon the crest, the armor-mantra between the two breasts using the two index fingers, and the eye-mantra upon the three eyes using the three middle fingers, as well as the weapon-mantra upon the palms of the hands; having performed the triple clapping of the hands (*tālatraya*) and the binding of the directions (*digbandha*); having consecrated [the self] with the root-mantra and performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*); one should contemplate oneself as Rudra, the Transcendent Consciousness (*manonmanī*). Thereafter, having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), and having first performed the placement of the *kalā*s of Gauri, one should perform the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).

Having washed the vessels for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and having filled them with the Heart-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*; having worshipped [the deity] with the seat (*āsana*), the form (*mūrtti*), the root-mantra (*mūla*), and the limbs (*aṅga*); having consecrated [the vessels] with the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*); having empowered them with the root-mantra and the limbs; having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and so forth; having displayed the cow’s teat (*gostanī*) and the womb (*yoni*) mudrās; having sprinkled the collection of substances for the offering (*arghya*) with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*); having consecrated it with the four purificatory rites; having duly worshipped oneself with the seat, the form, and the root-mantra; and having uttered the root-mantra—[one should perform] the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*).

...having performed [this], the *pañcagavya* should be prepared. Having worshipped Vighneśvara upon the *udumbara* wood above the gateway arch (*toraṇa*), one should worship Mahālakṣmī and Sarasvatī on the right and left [sides] of the center. On the right and left sides of the southern door-panel, one should worship Gaṅgā and Yoginī; on the left and right sides of the northern door-panel, Yamunā and Ḍākinī. On the right and left door-panels... [the rest follows].

Having offered water for the feet, water for sipping, and the *arghya* offering—along with sandalwood paste, flowers, incense, and so forth—to the Sindhu and Godāvarī rivers at the base of the *udumbara* tree in front of the altar, and having dispelled the three obstacles with the *mūla*, *astra*, and *pāśupatāstra* mantras while taking refuge slightly on the left branch, he enters within, stepping forward with his right foot. Having worshipped the *astradvārapāla* at the threshold with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the *astradvārapāla*," he worships Vāstu-Brahmā in the southwest (*nairṛta*).

Having worshipped Manonmanī with the Gāyatrī of Gaurī, having offered incense, lamps, and the *arghya* offering, having discarded the remains of the previous worship (*nirmālya*), and having sprinkled [the area] with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should offer the *āvāhana*, *sthāpana*, *sannidhāna*, *sannirodhana*, and the welcoming *arghya*. Then, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart and other limbs—though lacking eyes—and of the head-position, one performs the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*).

Having performed [the preliminary rites], having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the guest-offering (*arghya*) with the mantra ending in *svāhā* preceded by *namaḥ*, having bathed [the deity] with cow-dung, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and so forth, as well as with scented water, having again offered water for sipping and the guest-offering, having wiped [the deity] with a fine cloth, and having adorned [the deity] with garments, perfumes, a crown, earrings, necklaces, armlets, sandalwood paste, garlands, and the like, having offered three handfuls of flowers with the root mantra, and having displayed the *dhenupadmayoni* mudrās, one should pray for the sake of the worship of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*).

Now, in the first enclosure (*āvaraṇa*): in the southeast, northeast, southwest, and east, at the bases of the petals, [one should worship] from the Heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) up to the Eye-mantra (*netra*). The other limbs (*aṅga*) are in the four cardinal directions. In the second enclosure: in the four cardinal directions starting from the east—[one worships] Śubhāśubhavatī and Japāsumālinī. In the third enclosure: in the directions starting from the east and northeast, [one worships] Vāmā and the other *Śaktis*. In the fourth enclosure: in the eight directions, [starting] from the northeast and southwest, [one worships] Brahmā and Mātrā.

In the fifth enclosure, one should worship Durga, Virabhadra, Vighnesha, and Ishvara in the directions starting from the east. Having worshipped Vrishabha, Vinayaka, Skanda, Shashthi, Chaturbhujamukhi, and Narasimha, and having offered the *arghya*, one should present to the Goddess a handful of flowers with the root mantra, as well as *arghya*, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), water for drinking, water for sipping (*ācamana*), and betel. One should then offer the *bali* to the retinue on the right and left door-frames and in front, as well as to Shankha and Nidhi in the directions starting from the east.

Jambhinī, Mohinī, Bhedinī, Ramaṇī, Bhadrakālī, Durgā, and Cāmuṇḍeśvarī. On the right side of the gopura, at the great seat (mahāpīṭha) of Daṇḍimuṇḍī, on the four petals starting from the east, and in the pericarp (karṇikā), one should worship the Mothers of the three worlds who have become the sky, and the supreme Mothers. Having performed the washing and sprinkling, the invocation, and having offered the water for the feet, the water for sipping, the guest-offering (arghya), fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, and mudrās, preceded by the bali offering, one should perform the offering of the arghya-water and the heart-gesture (hṛdayāñjali). Afterwards, having entered the kitchen, one should perform the daily rites at the yoni-fire pit.

[One should offer] the *karmadevīs*... incense, lamps, the *ārātrika* [ceremony], sacred ash, mirrors, umbrellas, chowries, and fans; likewise, having offered the recitation (*vijñāpana*) of the heart-mantras, the *Āgama*s, the Vedic hymns (*sūkta*), the *Purāṇa*s, and the *Aṅga*s... having performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, having concluded it in the left hand, and having recited the mantras ten times the number of that [recitation], [one should offer] the food offering (*naivedya*). Having worshipped with eight flowers... having given [these], one should perform hymns of praise, circumambulation, and prostrations. Then, having invoked [the deity], one should say, "Forgive me."

One should worship with the root mantra. Having offered the *arghya* facing away [from oneself], one should expel obstacles from the world with the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*. One should unite the form with the *mūrti-mantra*, and contemplate the identity [of the deity] with the root mantra itself. Having worshipped and performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and so forth, one should recite the mantras for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the other offerings. Then, having approached the abode of Caṇḍeśvarī, one should worship her with the root mantra while holding the *arghya* in hand, and then dismiss her. Having bathed [the image], one should worship that seat with the root mantra, the *mūrti-mantra*, and the limb mantras (*aṅga*). Having offered the water for the feet and the other offerings, one should present the *nirmālya* (remnants of the previous offering).

The offerings (*nivedya*) have been presented. Having given the water for sipping (*ācamana*) and the respectful offering (*arghya*), one should withdraw that *arghya*. Thus ends the procedure for worship in *Manonmanī*. May there be auspiciousness! May there be success through the compassionate glance of Sarasvatī. Salutations to the venerable Agastyeśvara, together with the venerable Ānandavallī. Salutations to Subrahmaṇya, together with Vallidevasenā. In the year named after Īśvara, in the month of Siṃha, on Thursday.

On the eighth day of the bright fortnight, under the Viśākhā nakṣatra, after fifteen ghaṭikās of the afternoon— at Sirukuṇḍram, Subrahmaṇyan Kośapeṭṭai, having been written and presented by Subrahmaṇya-guru— this manual for the performance of the *parārthapūjā* has been completed.
